reference.source: Neurology textbooks and peer-reviewed leukodystrophy reviews
clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive leukodystrophy caused by biallelic variants in any of the five genes encoding subunits of eukaryotic translation initiation factor 2B (EIF2B1-5)

Hallmark clinical feature is episodic, stepwise neurological deterioration provoked by febrile illness, minor head trauma, or acute fright, often with marked lethargy or coma out of proportion to the trigger
Cerebellar ataxia and spasticity dominate the motor picture, whereas cognitive function is relatively spared until late

Classic childhood-onset form is most common, but the phenotype spans an antenatal/infantile severe end through to adult-onset and an ovarioleukodystrophy variant with premature ovarian failure in females

MRI shows diffuse, symmetrical white-matter abnormality that progressively rarefies and takes on cerebrospinal-fluid-like signal on all sequences, with a radiating stripe pattern of relatively preserved tissue
FLAIR sequences are especially useful, showing the affected white matter becoming suppressed (dark) as it liquefies, distinguishing it from simple demyelination
Confirmation is by molecular genetic testing of the EIF2B genes; there is no curative treatment, and management centres on avoiding known triggers
Families should be counselled to seek early care and antipyresis during infections and to minimise head injury, as these precipitate crises
reference.pathophysiology: Vanishing white matter disease results from loss-of-function variants in the genes encoding the five subunits of eukaryotic translation initiation factor 2B (eIF2B), a guanine-nucleotide exchange factor central to the regulation of protein synthesis, particularly under cellular stress. Impaired eIF2B activity deranges the integrated stress response, leaving glial cells (especially astrocytes and oligodendrocytes) unable to adapt to metabolic stresses such as fever, inflammation, or trauma. The result is progressive cerebral white-matter breakdown with abnormal, immature astrocytes and dysmyelination, so that the white matter gradually rarefies and cavitates into a fluid-like state while grey matter is comparatively preserved.
additionalDifferentials: Metachromatic leukodystrophy and other lysosomal leukodystrophies
Acute disseminated encephalomyelitis or post-infectious demyelination
Cerebral folate deficiency and other treatable metabolic leukoencephalopathies
additionalInvestigations: Brain MRI with FLAIR and T2 sequences to demonstrate diffuse white-matter rarefaction with progressive CSF-like signal
Molecular genetic testing of EIF2B1-5 to confirm the diagnosis
Metabolic screen to exclude other leukodystrophies (arylsulfatase A, very-long-chain fatty acids, lactate)
Serial neuroimaging to document progression and cavitation of white matter
Endocrine assessment of ovarian function in affected females (ovarioleukodystrophy variant)
redFlags: Rapid decline into stupor or coma following a febrile illness or minor head injury
Acute loss of previously acquired motor milestones after a trigger event
Status epilepticus or intractable seizures during an episode of deterioration
Signs of raised intracranial pressure or brainstem dysfunction during a crisis
reference.prognosis: The disorder is progressive and currently incurable; the classic childhood form typically causes stepwise decline with death within a few years of onset, whereas later-onset forms progress more slowly. Prognosis is strongly influenced by age at onset, with the earliest-onset presentations carrying the worst outlook.
pitfalls: Attributing a post-febrile collapse to encephalitis or sepsis alone and missing the underlying leukodystrophy
Misreading early MRI as ordinary demyelination and failing to recognise the FLAIR suppression that signals white-matter liquefaction
Overlooking premature ovarian failure as a clue in adolescent or adult females
Failing to counsel families about trigger avoidance, prompt antipyresis, and head-injury prevention
references: Adams and Victor's Principles of Neurology
GeneReviews: Childhood Ataxia with Central Nervous System Hypomyelination / Vanishing White Matter
management: No curative therapy; care is supportive with strict avoidance of the stress triggers that provoke deterioration
Prompt, aggressive management of febrile illness with antipyretics and early antibiotics, together with head-injury precautions
Perioperative and vaccination planning to reduce stress-related decompensation
Physiotherapy, occupational therapy and antispasticity treatment such as baclofen for ataxia and spasticity, with mobility and communication aids
Anticonvulsants for seizures and management of feeding difficulties, including gastrostomy where needed
Endocrine review and hormone replacement for premature ovarian failure in affected females
Multidisciplinary neurodisability support with palliative care in advanced disease
Autosomal recessive genetic counselling, EIF2B testing and cascade family screening
